result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.dispersion()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate dispersion between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19658-L19777){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.dispersion( u, v, normalized=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Dispersion](/assets/graphs/dispersion.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes A and B are outlined in the accent color and share three neighbors C, D, and E, filled in accent. C and D are linked, but E touches neither, so two of the three shared-neighbor pairs are unlinked: dispersion 2 / 3 = 0.667." width="100%"} Dispersion measures the embeddedness of a link in the network. A link between two nodes (`u` and `v`) has high dispersion when their mutual neighbors (friends in common) are not well connected to each other. This can indicate structural diversity in the network. The computation first collects the common neighbors of `u` and `v`. It then looks at every pair `(s, t)` of those common neighbors and counts the pair as *dispersed* when `s` and `t` are not adjacent and also have no neighbor in common other than `u` and `v` (i.e., they are more than two hops apart once `u` and `v` are set aside). The raw dispersion is the number of dispersed pairs; the normalized version divides it by the number of common neighbors. Dispersion is useful for: - identifying especially strong or intimate ties, such as partners or close family, which tend to connect otherwise separate social circles - distinguishing ties that sit inside one tight cluster from ties that span several - complementing plain overlap measures like `common_neighbors()`, which can't tell these two situations apart Things to keep in mind: `u` and `v` do not need to be adjacent; if they have fewer than two common neighbors the result is `0.0`. The measure is designed for undirected graphs. For directed graphs, neighbors are the outgoing neighbors of each node. The cost grows with the square of the number of common neighbors, which is negligible for typical pairs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [u]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first node of the pair, given as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). [v]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second node of the pair, given as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). The result is symmetric in `u` and `v` for undirected graphs. [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), divide the count of dispersed pairs by the number of common neighbors of `u` and `v` (their embeddedness), which makes scores easier to compare across ties with different numbers of mutual friends. If `False`, return the raw count of dispersed pairs (as a float). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The dispersion score between `u` and `v`. `0.0` when they share fewer than two neighbors or when all their shared neighbors are closely connected. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `u` or `v` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Dispersion, introduced by Backstrom and Kleinberg (2014), asks a subtler question than raw neighbor overlap: given the common neighbors of two nodes, how *dispersed* are they across the rest of the network? If the shared neighbors are themselves tightly interlinked, the tie between $u$ and $v$ sits in a dense cluster and dispersion is low; if those neighbors are far from one another in the residual graph, the tie spans different regions and dispersion is high. That property made it strikingly effective in its original application, spotting romantic partners in social-network data, where such ties bridge otherwise distinct friendship circles even when embeddedness is high. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `U` and `V` share three neighbors: `A`, `B`, and `C`. `A` and `B` know each other, but `C` is linked to neither, so two of the three shared-neighbor pairs (`A`-`C` and `B`-`C`) are dispersed, giving `2 / 3`: ::: {#5ffa061a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["U", "V", "A", "B", "C"]) graph.add_edges( [ ("U", "V"), ("U", "A"), ("U", "B"), ("U", "C"), ("V", "A"), ("V", "B"), ("V", "C"), ("A", "B"), ] ) round(graph.dispersion("U", "V"), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.667 ``` ::: ::: `normalized=False` returns the raw number of dispersed pairs instead of dividing it by the three common neighbors: ::: {#622ee484 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.dispersion("U", "V", normalized=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2.0 ``` ::: ::: Adding a node `X` that links `B` and `C` gives them a shared neighbor outside the `U`-`V` tie, so the `B`-`C` pair no longer counts and dispersion drops to `1 / 3`: ::: {#4b5d7f46 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_node(label="X") graph.add_edge("B", "X").add_edge("C", "X") round(graph.dispersion("U", "V"), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.333 ``` ::: ::: Ties inside a densely knit group have low dispersion. In a complete graph every pair of shared neighbors is directly linked, so the score is `0.0`: ::: {#e45b845b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} clique = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_full_graph(5) clique.dispersion(1, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0.0 ``` ::: :::
